items.title: Jimmy Owens interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001
items.q: I had the appreciation for the Clifford Browns and the Miles Davis and Dizzy Gillespies, you know, and the Freddie Hubbard

ctx.x: And seriously, I guess the defining moment was when I started to play the instrument. Because it was from that point on that I had the feeling that I wanted to be a professional musician. And that was at age ten. By the time I was fourteen I really had the feeling inside that I wanted to be a professional musician. And at sixteen I auditioned and got into the Newport Youth Band. It was run by Marshall Brown, and that kind of put the top on the lid from the standpoint of being a professional musician. The training…

second year in the school and I was in the Newport Youth Band, and we would have to stay off from school sometimes Mondays and Fridays, because we had concerts. And we had the greatest musicians teaching us. So that all added up to giving me a good insight on wanting to be a professional musician. My chief mentor at the time was Donald Byrd. I studied with him when I was fourteen years old. And living in New York, growing up in New York, at fourteen and fifteen I was hanging out in the clubs. And a lot of the…

items.title: Jimmy Owens interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001
items.q: playing music of the masters that I’ve arranged, music that I’ve collected over the years, original arrangements that I own by Benny Golson, by Dizzy Gillespie

ctx.x: Wow. What’s on your plate these days?

Well I’ve been a band leader since 1969. I haven’t been leading a band now for about seven, eight years. I’ve been doing projects, the kind of projects I like, along with other people. I stopped leading the band because I was just tired. From 1976 to about 1981, I was very busy with my band, performing in some of the most unknown places of the world where jazz has never been live. I did concerts in places like Nicaragua and El Salvador and Belize and Honduras and Senegal and Khartoum and the Middle East. Some of…
You’re not the first person who I’ve heard say that actually.

items.title: Jimmy Owens — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I met Dizzy in 1959, the first time.

ctx.x: He was a very fine trumpet player out of Dizzy Gillespie. He’s traditional. He didn’t have the chop and the strength that Dizzy had, you know, but he played that kind of stuff on the instrument. He was a good trumpet player.
And he and Charles McPherson together…
